title: Capt. William Hubbell’s Ohio Flatboat Stand (1791)
summary: On March 23, 1791, Capt. William Hubbell and his armed men fought off three Indian canoes while taking a flatboat down the Ohio toward Limestone.
bodyMarkdown:
In the spring of 1791 the Ohio River was still a war road. Northwestern nations were fighting American settlement north of the river, and boats carrying families to Kentucky were frequent targets. That year Capt. William Hubbell, of the Frankfort frontier, was bringing a flatboat down the Ohio toward Kentucky with a party of emigrants.

His boat carried about twenty people after several late pickups along the way, including Daniel Light, William Plascut and his family, and other men, women, and children. Only nine of the men were armed and fit to fight. Hubbell organized them anyway, dividing the guns and assigning posts in case of attack.

At dawn on March 23, 1791, near the Kanawha country, three large canoes full of warriors closed on the boat. Hubbell's men held a running fight from behind the boat's walls. When a ball smashed the lock of his rifle, Hubbell kept fighting. He used a burning stick from the fire to touch off another shot. When warriors tried to board, he drove them back with pistols and pieces of firewood, even after a bullet tore through his right arm.

The canoes finally turned away to chase easier prey. A second flatboat traveling nearby under Capt. Greathouse had not prepared to fight. It was taken ashore, and most of the people aboard were killed or carried off.

Hubbell's boat drifted on with its wounded. Two of his men died in the fight, and a third died later at Limestone. The women and children came through alive. The party reached Limestone, today's Maysville, that night, and by his own account the townspeople came down to the landing to see the boat, its sides full of bullet holes.

Hubbell lived on in Kentucky. His own narrative, printed long afterward, is the main source for the fight.

## Kentucky today

Limestone is now [Maysville](/stories/the-maysville-road-and-jacksons-veto-1830/) in Mason County. The riverfront where Hubbell's battered boat landed is lined with floodwall murals that tell the town's river history.
Source: [Narrative of the captivity of Capt. William Hubbell (Access Genealogy)](https://accessgenealogy.com/kentucky/narrative-captivity-capt-william-hubbell-indian-captivities.htm)
